answer: Before the twentieth century a victor in war could acquire title to land by conquest. That began to change with the 1928 Kellogg-Briand Pact, and the UN Charter of 1945 (Article 2(4)) forbade force against a state's territorial integrity. The Fourth Geneva Convention (1949, Article 49) bars forcible transfers from occupied territory. Security Council Resolution 242 (1967) stressed "the inadmissibility of the acquisition of territory by war", the 1970 Friendly Relations Declaration said no territorial acquisition by force shall be recognized as legal, and forcible transfer is now a crime against humanity under the Rome Statute. In the 1940s transfers were common, and the Allies approved some at Potsdam. Comparing cases explains the period; it does not answer whether a specific act was just.

contested: Whether comparisons excuse: critics of such comparisons, summarised by Michael Koplow of the Israel Policy Forum as the charge of "whataboutism", say pointing to other cases deflects from the act in question and treats worse conduct elsewhere as a defence. The card does not use the comparisons that way.

The counter-argument is a double standard: Cary Nelson and Michael Saenger (Fathom) argue that comparing Israel with other countries is normal practice in political science, that labelling the 1948 transfers "ethnic cleansing" while the millions of Europeans moved in the same years are not so labelled singles Israel out, and that the term "whataboutism" is used both to dismiss legitimate criticism and to dismiss legitimate comparison.

Whether the German case is a fair parallel: in the Israel Law Review discussion, a participant said the Sudeten expulsion was a punishment of the defeated carried out under a peace agreement, which was not the case in 1948; Benny Morris replied he cited it to show how the world then judged transfers, not to justify them.

Resolution 242: Ruth Lapidoth (Jerusalem Center for Public Affairs) argues the phrase in the preamble concerns acquisition of title, not military occupation, and that the preamble is not binding; Michael Lynk (Journal of Palestine Studies) argues the resolution endorses the inadmissibility of acquisition and calls for withdrawal. Both are cited above.
The law on conquest: Brunk and Hakimi (AJIL) argue that Article 2(4) regulates the use of force while the separate prohibition of annexation regulates title, and that the two are not the same.

not_claimed: That because transfers were common and accepted in the 1940s, any of them was just.
That Article 49 and the Rome Statute apply to 1948: the Convention is from 1949 and the Statute from 1998, and the card does not say they apply to events before them.
That Resolution 242 is binding law or that it settles the status of any territory; the card quotes its words and records the dispute.
That singling out one case is always a double standard, or that comparison is always whataboutism; both arguments are stated and neither is endorsed.
